statements.quote: Given a probability distribution over the next token, which one do you pick?
This is the **decoding strategy**, and it controls the model's “personality”, focused and deterministic, or wild and creative.
The frontier in 2025: many subtle techniques beyond temperature and top-$k$.

This chapter covers every common decoding method with its mathematical formulation and recommended use, grouped from the baseline distribution, through the candidate-set filters, to the diversity and search tricks and the practical settings that tie them together.
Three of the four quantities in this chapter, **Boltzmann distributions**, **entropy**, and **KL-divergence**, were born long before language models.
They appear in the Statistics II chapter § Boltzmann Distributions, § Entropy, § KL Divergence.
If softmax + temperature looks familiar from physics, that is because it *is* physics.

The softmax with temperature $T$ is exactly the **Boltzmann distribution** (\cite[Boltzmann, 1877]{boltzmann}) over the token "energy levels" $E_i = -z_i$ (the logit, negated), written in dimensionless form by absorbing the Boltzmann constant into $T$: $\;P_i = e^{z_i/T} / \sum_j e^{z_j/T}$.
So $T$ is not a knob we invented — it is a **temperature** in the thermodynamic sense.
$T \to 0$ is the **ground state**: the system collapses onto the single lowest-energy, highest-probability token (greedy).
$T \to \infty$ is the **infinite-temperature** limit, where every state is equally populated (uniform).
Raising $T$ does not make the model "creative" in any vague sense; it lets higher-energy, rarer tokens be occupied at all, the way a hotter gas puts its particles into excited states.
Sampling is thermodynamics in disguise.
Boltzmann's 1877 memoir gave the combinatorial derivation behind the distribution $p_i\propto e^{-E_i/kT}$ for a gas in thermal equilibrium (\cite{boltzmann}).

Gibbs gave the ensemble formulation in his 1902 treatise (\cite{gibbs1902}), and the same exponential family reappears as the Gibbs distribution in statistics and image processing (\cite{geman1984gibbs}).
Ackley, Hinton, and Sejnowski imported the idea into neural networks as the Boltzmann machine, where temperature controls the sharpness of the stochastic units (\cite{ackley1985boltzmann}).
Softmax temperature is exactly this formula with the negative logit playing the role of energy, so the analogy is structural, not decorative.
After the LLM produces logits $\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^{|V|}$ for the next token, softmax gives a probability distribution:
where $T$ is **temperature**:
* $T \to 0$: argmax (greedy).
Always picks the most likely token.
* $T = 1$: native distribution.
* $T \to \infty$: uniform distribution (random).
* $T > 1$: flatter distribution (more diverse, more random).
* $T < 1$: sharper distribution (more focused).
But that's only the beginning.
Most modern systems use **additional filters** on top of temperature.
Always pick $\arg\max_i P(i)$.
Used in production for fact-retrieval tasks where creativity is unwanted.
Drawback: **repetition loops** and **mode collapse** (“the the the the...”).
Restrict to the $k$ tokens with highest probability, then renormalize (\cite[Fan et al., 2018]{fan2018topk}):
where $Z = \sum_{j \in \mathcal{V}_k} P(j)$.
* $k = 50$: typical for chat.
* $k = 1000+$ for creative writing.
Drawback: $k$ is a fixed number, but the appropriate $k$ varies per context.
Sometimes only 3 tokens have meaningful probability; sometimes 100.
Fan, Lewis, and Dauphin introduced top-$k$ sampling for open-ended story generation, where pure ancestral sampling drifted into incoherence and beam search produced bland text (\cite{fan2018topk}).
Their model used $k=10$ together with a temperature, and the combination was enough to keep generations on topic without collapsing to the mode.
The method's weakness was visible from the start: a fixed $k$ cannot know whether the next distribution is sharp or flat, which is exactly the problem nucleus sampling later addressed.
Sample from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds $p$ (\cite[Holtzman et al., 2020]{holtzman2020nucleus}):
* $p = 0.9$: typical for chat (sample from top 90% of mass).
* $p = 0.95$: more diverse.
* $p = 0.5$: very focused.
This adapts the effective vocabulary size to the distribution.
When the distribution is sharp (one token dominates), $\mathcal{V}_p$ is small; when flat, $\mathcal{V}_p$ is large.
Most production APIs default to **top-$p$ = 0.9 or 0.95**.

Holtzman et al. diagnosed the failure of maximization-based decoding as a mismatch between machine and human text: greedy and beam search produce high-probability, low-surprisal strings that loop, while pure sampling occasionally goes off the rails (\cite{holtzman2020nucleus}).
Nucleus sampling keeps the smallest set of tokens whose mass reaches $p$, so the candidate pool expands when the model is uncertain and contracts when it is confident.
Human evaluation showed it matching or beating top-$k$ on coherence and diversity; the cost is that $p$ still has to be tuned per model.
A newer dynamic-truncation method (\cite[Nguyen et al., 2025]{nguyen2025minp}), available in Hugging Face Transformers, vLLM, and llama.cpp:
* Choose $m = \max_i P(i)$ (the highest probability).
* Include all tokens with $P(i) \geq s \cdot m$ where $s \in [0, 1]$ is the min-$p$ parameter.
* $s = 0.1$: include any token within 10× of the max.
* $s = 0.05$: more inclusive.
* $s = 1.0$: greedy (only the top token qualifies).
$s = 0.0$ switches the filter off (keeps every token).
Min-$p$ **scales with confidence**: when the model is sharp, few tokens qualify; when uncertain, more.
The authors report better quality and diversity than top-$p$, especially at higher temperatures; the evidence is strongest in that high-temperature regime.
Top-$n$ is just another name for top-$k$: keep exactly the $n$ highest-probability tokens, then renormalize.
The two names appear in different codebases, which can make them look like separate algorithms.
They are the same filter, and the same drawback applies: $n$ does not adapt to how sharp or flat the distribution is.
Discards tokens in the “tail” of the distribution where the second derivative of probability is small.
Rarely used in production.
Similar to min-$p$ but with a different criterion: cut off tokens with probability below an $\eta$-dependent threshold based on entropy.
Generally less popular than min-$p$.

Locally typical sampling starts from an information-theoretic observation: human text keeps each word's surprisal close to the conditional entropy of its context, while high-probability machine text is too predictable and pure sampling is too noisy (\cite{meister2022typical}).
The method keeps tokens whose information content $-\log p_i$ is closest to the entropy $H$, rather than the tokens with the largest probability.
On summarization and story generation it reduced repetition and scored competitively with nucleus sampling.
Its parameter is the mass $\tau$ of the typical set, so like top-$p$ it controls how much of the distribution survives.
Every method above is a different way of answering the same question: *which candidates are still allowed?* Below, a model has produced logits for the next word.
Turn the temperature, switch the filters on and off, and sample.
The faint bar behind each token is its probability after temperature; the bright bar is what is left after the filters cut the tail and the survivors are renormalized.
Then switch to the factual prompt and notice how top-$k$ keeps nonsense while top-$p$ and min-$p$ shrink to a single word on their own.
Penalize tokens that have already appeared in the context (\cite[Keskar et al., 2019]{keskar2019ctrl}).

CTRL divides their logits by $\theta$ inside the softmax; most implementations use the sign-aware form, which divides positive logits and multiplies negative ones so that every repeated token really becomes less likely:
* $\theta = 1.0$: no penalty.
* $\theta = 1.1$: mild penalty.
* $\theta = 1.3$: strong penalty.
Useful for chat where the model might otherwise loop.
OpenAI-style **frequency** and **presence** penalties are additive variants: subtract $\alpha\cdot\text{count}(i)$ or $\beta\cdot\mathbf{1}[i\in\text{context}]$ from the logit.
A smarter repetition penalty (Cohere, 2023) that detects repeated n-grams and penalizes them only when they would create a degenerate loop:
* Match n-grams of length $n \geq n_{\text{min}}$ (e.g., 8).
* If the most recent n-gram matches an earlier one and would continue the repetition, apply penalty.
More nuanced than the basic repetition penalty.
Used in Cohere's Command-R and recommended for long-context generation.
A 2024 technique: randomly exclude the top token from sampling with some probability.
Forces the model to use less-likely words.
Useful for breaking out of repetitive patterns in creative writing.
* $p_{\text{exclude}} = 0.1$: 10% of the time, the top token is excluded.
Contrastive search (\cite[Su et al., 2022]{su2022contrastive}) is a **deterministic** decoding strategy that picks the token maximizing:
where $\mathbf{h}_i$ is the token's hidden state and $\alpha$ controls the degeneration penalty.
The original objective uses the model probability $P(i)$, not its logarithm; replacing $P$ with $\log P$ changes the balance between confidence and the degeneration penalty.
Produces high-quality, **non-repetitive** output without randomness.
A sampling scheme (\cite[Basu et al., 2020]{basu2020mirostat}) that **targets a fixed perplexity** during generation.
The model adjusts its sampling to maintain target surprise:
* Target perplexity $\tau$ (e.g., $\tau = 5$).
* After each generated token, compute current perplexity.
* Adjust $k$ (top-$k$) to drive perplexity toward $\tau$.
Produces output with consistent information density.
Used by some LLM writers for creative prose.
Maintain the top $B$ partial sequences at each step; expand all of them; keep the top $B$.
Used in machine translation; rarely in modern LLM chat.
Drawbacks: tends to produce generic, “averaged” outputs in open-ended generation.
Beam search predates neural language models: speech recognizers such as Harpy pruned a tree of acoustic hypotheses with it in the 1970s (\cite{lowerre1976harpy}).

Sutskever et al. brought it into sequence-to-sequence translation, where it became the default because it searches sequence likelihood more thoroughly than greedy decoding (\cite{sutskever2014seq2seq}).
The catch is length: raw log-probabilities favor short outputs, so implementations divide by a length penalty.
In open-ended generation, that same likelihood objective rewards generic continuations, which is why chat models moved away from beam search.

The sampling rule at the heart of speculative decoding (\cite[Leviathan et al., 2023]{leviathan2023speculative}): the draft model proposes tokens probabilistically, the target model verifies them, and rejected proposals are corrected by sampling from the target's adjusted distribution:
This guarantees the output distribution exactly matches the target model's distribution, while achieving speedup.
| Use case | Temperature | Top-$p$ | Min-$p$ | Repetition penalty |
| **Creative writing** | 1.2 | 0.95 | 0.1 | 1.2 + DRY |
**Model-card defaults vary**: Qwen3 recommends temperature 0.6–0.7 with top-$p$ 0.8–0.95 and min-$p$ 0; DeepSeek-R1 recommends 0.6 with top-$p$ 0.95; Mistral cards do not set min-$p$ either.
The OpenAI API defaults to temperature 1.0 and top-$p$ 1.0; Anthropic likewise applies no nucleus truncation by default.
Product UIs may layer their own presets.
Min-$p$ is a common optional filter, not a universal default.
A 2024 idea: adjust temperature based on the entropy of the predicted distribution.
When the model is confident (low entropy), lower temperature; when uncertain (high entropy), raise it.
The intuition: respect the model's confidence rather than always applying the same temperature.
Implementations: **entropy-aware sampling** (\cite[Wang et al., 2024]{wang2024entropy}), **DynTemp**, and proprietary variants in vLLM and llama.cpp.
Not yet standardized but promising.
* **Reproducibility**: set temperature = 0 (or very low) for reproducible outputs.
* **For evals**: temperature = 0 + greedy.
Otherwise the eval is noisy.
* **For chat**: temperature 0.7–1.0, top-$p$ 0.9.
* **For code**: low temperature, no top-$p$, possibly beam search.
* **For batch inference**: deterministic, greedy.
A common mistake: using temperature 1.0 with top-$p$ 0.9 AND min-$p$ 0.05.
These compound; the effective sampling becomes very restricted.
**Pick one filter method** unless you know what you're doing.

The choice between greedy and stochastic decoding is not a binary of correct versus creative (\cite{fan2018topk, holtzman2020nucleus}); temperature 0 removes sampling noise but not every source of variation.
Floating-point reductions, GPU kernel scheduling, batching, and tensor-parallel order can change the last bits of a logit, and a near-tie can then flip the argmax.
Providers that offer a seed make a best effort, not a guarantee.
The practical rule is to fix sampler, seed, model version, and batch shape together; if an evaluation must be exactly repeatable, cache the generated outputs rather than regenerate them.
